blocks.explanation: After the 1992 testing moratorium, the US shifted to Stockpile Stewardship — using supercomputer simulations to verify aging warheads still work without detonating them.

timeline.heading: HIGH-VALUE TARGET
timeline.body: The attorney's phrase is a term of art. Facilities tied to nuclear weapons infrastructure fall under Department of Energy security protocols and become potential targets in any great-power conflict. A township hosting such a site inherits risk without controlling it — no local zoning board can approve or refuse the targeting calculus.

timeline.heading: THE GREAT LAKES PARADOX
timeline.body: Michigan sits on 20% of the world's surface freshwater, yet the Great Lakes Compact (2008) restricts diversions outside the basin and gives local governments veto power over large withdrawals. Abundance at the watershed scale does not translate to unlimited extraction at the parcel scale — a lesson Phoenix and Las Vegas learned earlier with groundwater.

timeline.heading: THE MORATORIUM PATTERN
timeline.body: Since 2023, dozens of US localities — from Chandler, Arizona to Peculiar, Missouri — have paused or rejected datacenter projects over water and power. The veto is rarely environmental alone; it is political. Residents see hyperscalers extracting infrastructure while contributing little to the property tax base after negotiated abatements.

timeline.heading: THE SHADOW FLEET
timeline.body: Iran moves sanctioned oil through a fleet of roughly 300 aging tankers that disable their AIS transponders, reflag mid-voyage, and conduct ship-to-ship transfers in the open ocean. The vessels are typically owned through shell companies in jurisdictions with minimal disclosure — Marshall Islands, St. Kitts, San Marino.

blocks.text: The industry term is *dark fleet* — tankers running with transponders off to obscure origin, destination, and cargo. Roughly **10%** of the global tanker fleet now operates this way, up from near zero a decade ago.

timeline.heading: THE LEGAL BASIS
timeline.body: US seizures of Iranian oil rely on civil forfeiture under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The government sues the cargo itself — in rem jurisdiction — arguing the oil is the proceeds of sanctions violations. The ship's owner must appear in US court to contest, which most shell companies will not do.

blocks.question: Under US civil forfeiture, who is the defendant when oil is seized from a sanctioned tanker?
blocks.explanation: In rem forfeiture treats the property as the defendant — the case is literally styled 'United States v. [the oil].' This bypasses the need to establish personal jurisdiction over foreign owners.

timeline.heading: THE CHINA CHANNEL
timeline.body: Roughly 90% of Iran's crude exports go to China, much of it labeled as Malaysian or Omani origin after ship-to-ship transfers near Singapore or in the Gulf of Oman. Independent Chinese refineries — teapots, concentrated in Shandong — are the primary buyers. State-owned majors avoid the trade to protect dollar access.

timeline.heading: THE INDIAN OCEAN PIVOT
timeline.body: Seizing tankers 2,000km from Hormuz signals a shift. Historical interdictions happened in the Gulf itself, where Iran could retaliate with fast-boat swarms. Open-ocean seizures push the contest into water where US carrier groups dominate and Iran has no practical reach.

blocks.label: the route east
blocks.caption: Hormuz to Chinese refineries via the Indian Ocean

timeline.heading: THE 1988 ECHO
timeline.body: Operation Praying Mantis in April 1988 sank half the Iranian navy in a single day after the USS Samuel B. Roberts struck an Iranian mine. The lesson Tehran drew was not to stop harassing shipping but to shift toward asymmetric tools — proxies, fast boats, mines — that avoid direct naval engagement with the US.

timeline.heading: THE PRICE FLOOR
timeline.body: Seizures remove physical barrels from the market but rarely move Brent more than a dollar or two. The shadow fleet has enough slack to reroute; buyers have enough alternative suppliers. The real pressure is on Iran's revenue per barrel — discounts to Chinese buyers now run $10-15 below Brent.

timeline.heading: THE COMPOUND MODEL
timeline.body: Scam compounds are industrial-scale fraud factories — guarded buildings where thousands of trafficked workers, often lured by fake job ads, are forced to run romance-investment scams on victims abroad. The business grew out of shuttered Chinese-run casinos in Cambodia and Myanmar after COVID border closures killed gambling tourism.

blocks.label: where the compounds cluster
blocks.caption: Southeast Asia's Mekong corridor hosts most known compounds

timeline.heading: PIG BUTCHERING
timeline.body: The Chinese term is sha zhu pan — 'fattening the pig before slaughter.' Operators build weeks of rapport with a target on dating apps or WhatsApp, then introduce a fake crypto investment platform. Small withdrawals succeed to build trust; when the victim commits serious money, the platform vanishes.

blocks.text: The FBI estimated Americans lost **$5.6 billion** to crypto investment fraud in 2023 alone — more than any other cybercrime category. The scale is driven by the compound model's ability to run *thousands* of conversations in parallel.

timeline.heading: HOW OFAC SANCTIONS WORK
timeline.body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control can freeze any assets touching the US financial system and bar Americans from any transaction with the target. Because nearly all dollar-clearing flows through US correspondent banks, an OFAC designation effectively cuts the target off from the global banking system — not just American banks.

blocks.question: What gives OFAC sanctions their global reach beyond US borders?
options: A UN Security Council mandate requires compliance
Nearly all US dollar transactions clear through US banks
Foreign banks voluntarily agreed by treaty
blocks.explanation: Dollar clearing runs through US correspondent banks, so any foreign bank that wants dollar access must honor OFAC — giving one country's sanctions list near-global effect.

timeline.heading: THE BNP PARIBAS LESSON
timeline.body: In 2014, BNP Paribas paid $8.9 billion for processing dollar transactions with sanctioned entities. The message to global banks was unambiguous: screen every dollar payment against OFAC's SDN list, or pay. This is why a single senator's name on the list can isolate him from institutions his own government still recognizes.

timeline.heading: THE JURISDICTION GAP
timeline.body: Cambodian law enforcement has rarely moved against compound operators, many of whom are politically connected or provide tax revenue to border provinces. UN estimates put compound-related fraud earnings across Southeast Asia at tens of billions annually — comparable to several countries' national budgets. The sanction targets someone the host state is unlikely to prosecute.

blocks.label: compound fraud earnings vs regional budgets

timeline.heading: WHY A SENATOR IS NOVEL
timeline.body: OFAC routinely targets traffickers, cartel figures, and oligarchs. Designating a sitting legislator of an allied-adjacent country is an escalation — it signals Treasury has concluded the political system itself is the enabling infrastructure, not a few rogue operators within it.

timeline.heading: THE MECHANISM
timeline.body: Pretrial detention — holding someone before trial — is meant to prevent flight or evidence tampering. In Egypt it has become the punishment itself: hold someone for years under 15-day extensions that require no verdict, no evidence threshold met in open court, and often no trial date.

blocks.text: The technical term is *habs ihtiyati* — **precautionary detention** — and Egyptian courts can renew it indefinitely in 15-day increments up to a two-year cap. The workaround: file a fresh case on the day the cap expires. Activists call this *tadwir* — **recycling**.

timeline.heading: THE RECYCLING TRICK
timeline.body: When the two-year legal maximum on pretrial detention approaches, prosecutors open a new case with fresh charges — often based on the same underlying conduct or on prison writings — and the clock resets. The detainee never leaves the cell; only the case file changes.

timeline.heading: THE 2014 CONSTITUTION
timeline.body: Egypt's post-Sisi constitution, ratified by referendum in January 2014, guarantees in Article 54 that pretrial detention must be exceptional and time-limited. The same document authorizes the emergency frameworks and military courts that make the guarantee unenforceable in practice.

blocks.text: Personal freedom is a natural right, safeguarded and inviolable. Except in cases of flagrante delicto, no person may be arrested, searched, detained, or have their freedom restricted except by a reasoned judicial order.
blocks.speaker: Egyptian Constitution, Article 54

timeline.heading: WHO DOUMA IS
timeline.body: A poet and activist, Douma was a lead organizer in the Tahrir Square protests that toppled Mubarak in 2011. He has been imprisoned under Mubarak, under the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, under Morsi, and under Sisi — the rare dissident jailed by every Egyptian regime of the last fifteen years.

timeline.heading: THE COHORT
timeline.body: Egyptian human rights groups estimate over 60,000 political prisoners, with tens of thousands held on recycled remand rather than after conviction. The strategy keeps conviction statistics low and trial dockets manageable while achieving indefinite incarceration.

blocks.question: What is the legal maximum for pretrial detention under Egyptian law before recycling resets it?
blocks.explanation: The Criminal Procedures Code caps pretrial detention at two years — prosecutors evade the cap by opening a new case on expiry, a practice known as tadwir (recycling).

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Indefinite detention without trial has a long colonial lineage in Egypt — the British-era 1914 Defence of Egypt Regulations, Nasser's 1958 emergency laws, Mubarak's 1981 state of emergency renewed every three years for thirty-one years. Sisi's recycling is the newest iteration of a mechanism the Egyptian state has rarely been without.

timeline.heading: THE IMPORT DEPENDENCY
timeline.body: Japan imports nearly all its crude oil and about 90% of it transits the Strait of Hormuz. No other G7 economy is this exposed to a single chokepoint — a Hormuz disruption passes through to Japanese prices faster than to any peer.

blocks.label: G7 crude from the Gulf (share of imports)

timeline.heading: WHY 2% IS THE WHOLE GAME
timeline.body: The BOJ fought deflation for a quarter-century. Hitting 2% inflation *sustainably* — driven by wages, not oil — is the condition for exiting the zero-rate era that began in 1999. Imported cost-push inflation is precisely the kind the BOJ has historically looked through.

blocks.text: The distinction matters: **demand-pull** inflation (wages, spending) signals a healthy economy; **cost-push** inflation (oil, freight) is a tax on consumers that fades once the shock passes. Raising rates against the latter crushes demand without fixing the cause.

timeline.heading: THE 1973 GHOST
timeline.body: The first oil shock tripled Japan's consumer price inflation to 23% in 1974 and ended the postwar miracle's double-digit growth era. The BOJ's institutional memory of that shock — and the stagflation it caused — shapes every decision when oil spikes today.

timeline.heading: THE YEN FEEDBACK LOOP
timeline.body: Oil is priced in dollars. When the yen weakens — as it has for years against a Fed holding rates higher — every barrel costs more yen even before the dollar price moves. A Hormuz shock and a weak yen compound into a double hit on Japanese households.

timeline.heading: WHAT A RATE HIKE ACTUALLY DOES
timeline.body: The BOJ's policy rate is 0.5% — still the lowest in the developed world. Raising it strengthens the yen (cheaper imports) but tightens credit for a debt-laden government whose interest burden scales with every basis point. Japan's debt-to-GDP is roughly 250% — the highest among major economies.

blocks.question: Why is raising rates especially costly for Japan's government?
options: Its debt-to-GDP is ~250%, the highest of any major economy
blocks.explanation: Every 1% rise in yields adds roughly 1% of GDP to interest costs over time — a brutal math problem at 250% debt-to-GDP.

timeline.heading: THE HORMUZ PASS-THROUGH
timeline.body: Freight and insurance premiums move within days of a chokepoint disruption; refined product prices follow in weeks; core CPI captures it months later. March's 42% jump in ocean freight is the leading edge of a wave that hasn't hit consumer shelves yet.

timeline.heading: WHAT DISTILLATION IS
timeline.body: A smaller 'student' model learns to mimic a larger 'teacher' by training on the teacher's outputs rather than the original data. The student ends up with much of the teacher's capability at a fraction of the parameters — and without ever seeing the weights.

blocks.text: The technique was formalized by Hinton in 2015 as *knowledge distillation* — originally a compression trick, now a geopolitical vector.

timeline.heading: WHY IT WORKS
timeline.body: Frontier models cost hundreds of millions to train from scratch — the expense is in the data curation, RLHF, and compute. But querying a trained model is cheap. Distillation converts the teacher's trillion-dollar training run into the student's million-dollar query bill.

blocks.label: training vs distilling a frontier model

timeline.heading: THE TERMS-OF-SERVICE SHIELD
timeline.body: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google all prohibit using their outputs to train competing models. This is contract law, not IP law — the underlying outputs are not copyrightable, so companies rely on API terms to block distillation. Enforcement requires catching the distiller, which is why proxy accounts matter.

timeline.heading: THE DEEPSEEK MOMENT
timeline.body: In January 2025, Chinese lab DeepSeek released R1, a reasoning model matching OpenAI's o1 at a claimed fraction of the training cost. US officials alleged it was distilled from OpenAI outputs. The episode made distillation a national-security concern, not a terms-of-service dispute.

timeline.heading: WHY PROXIES MATTER
timeline.body: A single account querying a frontier model millions of times trips rate limits and abuse detection. Tens of thousands of proxy accounts, each making modest queries, reconstruct a full behavioral map of the teacher without tripping any single threshold. The technique is the AI-era version of the smurf — transaction structuring for model weights.

blocks.question: Why can't API providers simply block distillation by detecting query patterns?
options: Distillation queries look like normal user traffic when spread across many accounts
Providers are legally required to serve all paying customers
Distillation requires access to model weights, not queries
blocks.explanation: Distributed across tens of thousands of accounts, distillation queries are statistically indistinguishable from ordinary usage — which is why detection relies on account provenance, not query content.

timeline.heading: THE ESPIONAGE RECLASSIFICATION
timeline.body: The Economic Espionage Act of 1996 covers trade secrets — information kept confidential and protected. Model behavior exposed through a public API is not obviously a trade secret. Reclassifying extraction as espionage would extend the statute into a new domain and is what Congress is now weighing.

timeline.heading: THE PARADOX
timeline.body: Australia is the world's second-largest LNG exporter, yet its east coast faces domestic gas shortages and some of the highest industrial gas prices in the OECD. The gas leaves the country faster than it can be reserved for local use.

timeline.heading: THE GIVEAWAY
timeline.body: The Petroleum Resource Rent Tax, designed in 1987 for offshore oil, allowed LNG projects to deduct exploration and construction costs at compounding rates. For roughly a decade after Gorgon and Wheatstone began shipping, the federal government collected almost no PRRT from LNG at all.

blocks.text: The deduction carry-forward rate was set at the **long-term bond rate plus 15%** — a number that made sense for risky 1980s oil exploration, and absurd for guaranteed-buyer LNG megaprojects.

timeline.heading: THE NORWAY CONTRAST
timeline.body: Norway taxes offshore petroleum at a combined rate near 78% and channels the proceeds into a sovereign wealth fund now worth over $1.7 trillion. Australia extracts comparable gas volumes and has no sovereign fund to show for it.

timeline.heading: WHO OWNS THE GAS
timeline.body: The major North West Shelf and Gorgon operators are foreign-headquartered — Chevron, ExxonMobil, Shell, Woodside (Australian), and INPEX. Most LNG leaves under long-term contracts to Japanese and Korean utilities, often at prices struck years before the 2022 energy spike.

timeline.heading: THE POLITICAL PHYSICS
timeline.body: Resource taxes are graveyards for Australian prime ministers. Kevin Rudd proposed a 40% Resource Super Profits Tax in 2010 and was removed by his own party within months after a mining-industry advertising blitz. Julia Gillard's watered-down replacement raised almost nothing and was repealed by Tony Abbott in 2014.

blocks.question: What happened to the Australian PM who proposed a 40% mining super-profits tax in 2010?
options: He passed it and won re-election
He was removed by his own party within months
He lost a general election to the opposition
He withdrew it and stayed in office
blocks.explanation: Kevin Rudd was ousted by Labor in June 2010 after a mining-industry campaign against the Resource Super Profits Tax — a precedent every Australian PM since has studied.

timeline.heading: THE DIATHESIS-STRESS MODEL
timeline.body: Schizophrenia is not caused by genes alone or by trauma alone. The dominant model since the 1970s holds that genetic vulnerability (diathesis) requires environmental stress to trigger expression. Identical twins share ~50% concordance, not 100% — the other half is environment.

blocks.text: The gap between genetic *loading* and actual *onset* is where childhood adversity does its work — and where this study claims to find the **molecular bridge**.

timeline.heading: WHAT LONG NON-CODING RNA DOES
timeline.body: Most of the human genome does not code for proteins. Long non-coding RNAs — transcripts over 200 nucleotides — regulate which genes get expressed, silenced, or amplified. They were dismissed as 'junk DNA' until the 2000s; now they are understood as the dimmer switches on the genome.

timeline.heading: WHY BLOOD MARKERS MATTER
timeline.body: Psychiatric diagnosis has always been behavioral — interviews, symptom scales, clinician judgment. There is no blood test for schizophrenia, no brain scan that confirms it. A peripheral biomarker measurable before psychosis onset would be the first objective early-warning tool in the field's history.

timeline.heading: THE CORTISOL PATHWAY
timeline.body: Chronic childhood stress elevates cortisol, which crosses the blood-brain barrier and remodels the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex — regions implicated in schizophrenia. The HPA axis (hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal) stays dysregulated into adulthood in many patients with psychotic disorders.

timeline.heading: THE PANSS SCALE
timeline.body: The Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale, developed in 1987, scores 30 symptoms on a 1–7 scale. 'Positive' symptoms are added experiences (hallucinations, delusions); 'negative' are subtractions (flat affect, social withdrawal). Most antipsychotics treat positive symptoms well and negative symptoms poorly — which is why schizophrenia remains so disabling.

blocks.question: Which type of schizophrenia symptoms do current antipsychotics treat most effectively?
blocks.explanation: Dopamine-blocking drugs dampen positive symptoms but do little for negative or cognitive ones — the main reason schizophrenia remains so disabling even with treatment.

timeline.heading: THE REPLICATION PROBLEM
timeline.body: Psychiatric genetics is littered with biomarkers that worked in one 400-person cohort and vanished in the next. The field's base rate for replication is low enough that even striking effect sizes (54.8%, 41.5%) should be held provisionally until independent samples confirm them.

timeline.heading: WHO COUPANG IS
timeline.body: Coupang is South Korea's dominant e-commerce platform — a Seoul-born, Delaware-incorporated company that listed on the NYSE in 2021 at a $60bn valuation. SoftBank's Vision Fund was the anchor investor; most of its equity sits with US institutional holders, which is why a Korean prosecution reads in Washington as an attack on American capital.

blocks.text: The structure matters: Coupang LLC is **Delaware-domiciled**, its operating subsidiary Coupang Korea is the one Seoul prosecutors can reach. This split is what makes the case an *investor-state* dispute rather than a domestic one.

timeline.heading: WHAT ISDS IS
timeline.body: Investor-state dispute settlement lets foreign investors sue a host government in international arbitration — bypassing that country's courts — when they believe state action has destroyed the value of their investment. The US-Korea FTA (KORUS, 2012) contains one of the broader ISDS clauses in the US treaty network.

blocks.question: Under KORUS ISDS, where would a US investor's claim against South Korea be heard?
blocks.explanation: ISDS routes claims to private arbitral tribunals — typically ICSID at the World Bank or under UNCITRAL rules — not to the host country's courts.

timeline.heading: THE BREACH SCALE
timeline.body: A breach of 33.7 million accounts in a country of 52 million is a near-total population exposure. Korea's Personal Information Protection Act allows fines up to 3% of related revenue and criminal liability for executives — the statutory hook prosecutors are using against the CEO.

timeline.heading: THE SUBMARINE LEVERAGE
timeline.body: The talks Washington is holding hostage concern a proposed South Korean nuclear-powered (not nuclear-armed) attack submarine — a capability currently confined to the US, UK, France, Russia, China, and India, with Australia pending under AUKUS. Korea wants the propulsion technology to counter Chinese and North Korean undersea activity; the US controls the enrichment and reactor-design transfers that would make it possible.

timeline.heading: THE PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Linking commercial prosecutions to security cooperation inverts the usual direction of alliance pressure. Washington historically invokes security leverage to push trade liberalization (Japan auto quotas, 1981) or sanctions compliance (EU-Iran, 2018). Using it to shield a specific executive from a specific domestic prosecution is unusual — and sets a template other allies will read carefully.

timeline.heading: WHY KOREA IS EXPOSED
timeline.body: South Korea runs a trade surplus with the US, hosts 28,500 US troops, and depends on the US nuclear umbrella against Pyongyang. It has less room to refuse than almost any other treaty ally — which is precisely why Washington is testing whether commercial protection can be extracted through security channels.

timeline.heading: THE BLUE LINE
timeline.body: The UN-demarcated 'Blue Line' between Lebanon and Israel was drawn in 2000 after Israel's withdrawal ending a 22-year occupation. It is not a border — Lebanon never formally accepted it — but a line of withdrawal that both sides have probed ever since.

timeline.heading: RESOLUTION 1701
timeline.body: The UN Security Council resolution that ended the 2006 war required Hezbollah to disarm south of the Litani River and Israel to withdraw fully. Neither happened. The resolution's unfulfilled text has been the reference point for every subsequent escalation, including the current one.

timeline.heading: THE SCORCHED BUFFER
timeline.body: Israel's historical response to cross-border fire has been to create a depopulated strip. The 'security zone' Israel maintained from 1985 to 2000 covered roughly 10% of Lebanese territory. Systematic demolition of border villages is the mechanism — render the land uninhabitable, and the threat moves back.

blocks.text: Military doctrine calls this *dahiya* — named after the 2006 flattening of Beirut's southern suburb — the principle that disproportionate destruction of civilian infrastructure deters the next round.

timeline.heading: SATELLITE AS WITNESS
timeline.body: Commercial imagery from Planet Labs and Maxar now refreshes daily at sub-meter resolution. For conflicts where journalists cannot enter, open-source analysts at outlets like Forensic Architecture and the BBC Verify unit have made satellite the default evidence layer — often confirming demolitions before residents learn of them.

blocks.question: How often do commercial satellite constellations now image most of Earth's land surface?
blocks.explanation: Planet Labs' SkySat and Dove constellations image the entire landmass daily at 3-meter resolution, with sub-meter tasking on demand.

timeline.heading: THE DISPLACEMENT MATH
timeline.body: 1.2 million displaced is roughly one in five Lebanese. The country was already absorbing 1.5 million Syrian refugees and had collapsed its currency by 98% since 2019. Each new shock layers onto a state that has not had a functioning president or budget for most of the past five years.

timeline.heading: THE CEASEFIRE ON PAPER
timeline.body: The November 2024 ceasefire required Israeli withdrawal within 60 days and Hezbollah's retreat north of the Litani. Israel retained five 'strategic points' past the deadline, citing ongoing threats. The pattern echoes the IRA precedent: armed groups disarm only when the political process delivers more than the armed struggle — and the sequence is ceasefire, politics, then decommissioning, never the reverse.

blocks.label: Israel x Hezbollah Ceasefire extended by…

timeline.heading: THE BLUE LINE
timeline.body: The UN drew the Blue Line in 2000 to certify Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon — not as a border, but as a withdrawal-verification line. It was never agreed bilaterally. Every Israeli presence south of the Litani since then has been measured against it, including the current 5-10km strip.

timeline.heading: RESOLUTION 1701
timeline.body: The 2006 war ended with UNSC Resolution 1701 demanding Hezbollah disarmament south of the Litani River and Israeli withdrawal to the Blue Line. Neither happened. Hezbollah rebuilt its arsenal; Israel retained overflight rights it still exercises daily. The current framework is built on a resolution that was never implemented.

blocks.text: The Litani is roughly **30km** north of the Israeli border. The zone between the river and the Blue Line was supposed to be weapons-free under **1701** — it became Hezbollah's densest fortification belt instead.

timeline.heading: THE SEQUENCING FIGHT
timeline.body: Israel's position — disarmament first, withdrawal second — inverts the standard conflict-termination sequence. Armed groups historically disarm only after political processes deliver alternatives; demanding disarmament as a precondition rather than an outcome is how ceasefires collapse.

blocks.question: How long did the IRA take to fully decommission its weapons after the Good Friday Agreement?
blocks.explanation: The IRA took 8 years and required independent verification. Armed groups disarm after political participation, not before — the sequence Israel is inverting in Lebanon.

timeline.heading: THE TAIF SETTLEMENT
timeline.body: The 1989 Taif Agreement ended Lebanon's civil war by disarming every militia — except Hezbollah, which was reclassified as a 'resistance' force because Israel still occupied the south. Hezbollah's arms have always been justified by Israeli presence. Each is the other's legitimacy.

timeline.heading: THE CURRENCY BACKDROP
timeline.body: Lebanon's state cannot coerce Hezbollah's disarmament because it barely functions. The pound lost more than 98% of its value since 2019; the banking sector is insolvent; electricity runs hours per day. A state this weak cannot absorb Hezbollah's social services, let alone its arsenal.

timeline.heading: THE ESCHATOLOGICAL GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: Southern Lebanon sits within al-Sham — the greater Levant — which multiple hadith in Sahih Muslim and Abu Dawud describe as a theatre of end-times events. Muslim readers encountering this file should understand that for many in the region, Lebanon is not merely a border dispute; it is sacred ground whose contestation carries theological weight beyond what diplomatic cables capture.

timeline.heading: WHAT TAU ACTUALLY DOES
timeline.body: Tau is a structural protein that stabilizes microtubules — the rails neurons use to ferry cargo from the cell body down the axon. When tau detaches and misfolds, the rails collapse and the neuron starves from the inside.

blocks.text: The healthy form is called *soluble tau*; the diseased form is *paired helical filaments* — twisted ribbons visible under electron microscopy since the 1960s.

timeline.heading: THE AMYLOID DEFEAT
timeline.body: For thirty years Alzheimer's research chased beta-amyloid plaques. Drug after drug cleared the plaques and failed to restore memory. The field has pivoted: tau tangles correlate with cognitive decline far better than amyloid load does.

timeline.heading: WHY AGGREGATION IS THE ENEMY
timeline.body: Misfolded proteins seed more misfolding — a prion-like chain reaction. One tau tangle templates the next, spreading cell-to-cell along connected circuits. This is why tauopathy follows predictable anatomical routes through the brain.

blocks.question: Which disease is NOT classified as a tauopathy?
blocks.explanation: Parkinson's is a synucleinopathy — driven by alpha-synuclein aggregates, not tau. CTE, Alzheimer's, and PSP all feature tau tangles as a primary lesion.

timeline.heading: WHAT BRICHOS IS
timeline.body: BRICHOS is a 100-residue protein domain found in a handful of unrelated human proteins, including lung surfactant protein C and tenomodulin. Its evolved function appears to be chaperoning — binding aggregation-prone surfaces on other proteins and keeping them soluble.

timeline.heading: THE DELIVERY PROBLEM
timeline.body: The blood-brain barrier blocks roughly 98% of small molecules and essentially all large proteins. Getting a therapeutic protein into mouse brain via IV is already hard; scaling to human brains — a thousand times larger, with decades of accumulated pathology — is the gap that kills most neurodegenerative candidates between mouse and clinic.

timeline.heading: THE MOUSE-TO-HUMAN CLIFF
timeline.body: Transgenic tauopathy mice overexpress a mutant human tau gene; their disease runs in months, not decades. Dozens of compounds have rescued memory in these mice and then failed human trials. The mouse is a mechanism test, not an efficacy prediction.

timeline.heading: THE MISMATCH
timeline.body: Corporate tax is territorial: you tax profit where the company has a physical presence. But a US tech firm can sell ads to UK users, book the revenue in Ireland, and pay almost no UK tax. DSTs are a workaround — tax the revenue where the users are, not where the profit is declared.

blocks.text: The UK's **2% levy** applies to revenue — not profit — from search, social media, and marketplaces with UK users. Revenue taxation bypasses the *transfer pricing* tricks that shrink declared profit to near zero.

timeline.heading: WHY 2%
timeline.body: DSTs are deliberately small. A 2% rate on revenue roughly approximates what a normal corporate tax would yield on the profit these firms actually earn in the country — if that profit were declared locally. Low enough to be defensible, high enough to raise real money: the UK DST collects around £800m a year.

timeline.heading: WHO PAYS THEM
timeline.body: Nearly all DST revenue globally comes from five American companies: Google, Meta, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft. No European or Asian firm has the scale to trigger the thresholds. This is what makes DSTs a transatlantic fight — they are, in practice, a tax that only US firms pay.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of global DST revenue is paid by US-headquartered companies?
blocks.explanation: The thresholds (typically €750m global revenue) exclude nearly all non-US digital firms; Alibaba and Tencent book little revenue in DST jurisdictions.

timeline.heading: THE OECD DEAL THAT STALLED
timeline.body: In 2021, 140 countries agreed an OECD framework — Pillar One — that would reallocate taxing rights on the largest multinationals, letting countries tax a slice of profit based on where users are. Countries agreed to drop DSTs once it took effect. It hasn't: the US Senate never ratified the underlying treaty, and the deal has been in limbo since.

timeline.heading: THE SECTION 301 PLAYBOOK
timeline.body: The US trade representative opened Section 301 investigations into DSTs under Trump's first term, finding them discriminatory against US firms. Biden suspended the retaliatory tariffs in 2021 pending the OECD deal. With Pillar One stalled and Trump back in office, the tariff threat is the original 2020 playbook, reactivated.

timeline.heading: WHY LONDON IS STUCK
timeline.body: Scrapping the DST costs the Treasury roughly £800m annually and looks like capitulation to Washington. Keeping it risks tariffs on UK exports — cars, Scotch, pharmaceuticals — that dwarf the tax's yield. France and Italy are watching: whichever country folds first sets the precedent for the rest.

timeline.heading: THE CITIZENS UNITED HINGE
timeline.body: Before 2010, corporations and unions were barred from independent political spending. Citizens United v. FEC reversed that, and the SpeechNow.org ruling weeks later let independent-expenditure committees raise unlimited sums. The super PAC was born in the gap between those two decisions.

blocks.text: A *super PAC* may raise unlimited money but cannot coordinate with a campaign. A traditional **PAC** is capped at $5,000 per donor but may give directly to candidates. The distinction is the entire architecture.

timeline.heading: THE PASS-THROUGH MECHANIC
timeline.body: Money routed from one PAC to another, then to a third, obscures the original donor on each subsequent disclosure. Each hop is legal under FEC rules; what regulators call 'earmarking' — explicit instructions tying a donation to a candidate — is the line that turns it into a violation.

blocks.question: What makes pass-through PAC funding legal rather than 'earmarking'?
options: The absence of explicit donor instructions tying the money to a candidate
Routing through at least three separate committees
Filing the transfer with the FEC within 48 hours
blocks.explanation: Earmarking — written or implied instructions linking a donation to a specific candidate — is the FEC's bright line. Without it, multi-hop transfers between independent PACs are permitted.

timeline.heading: WHY AIPAC BUILT A SUPER PAC
timeline.body: For decades AIPAC operated as a lobbying organization that did not endorse candidates or spend on elections. In 2021 it launched the United Democracy Project, its first super PAC, and AIPAC PAC, a traditional PAC. The shift made it one of the largest single-issue spenders in Democratic primaries within two cycles.

blocks.label: top single-issue super PAC spending, 2024 cycle

timeline.heading: THE PRIMARY THEORY OF CHANGE
timeline.body: General-election seats in safely partisan districts are decided in the primary. A super PAC that drops $2-5M in a low-turnout primary can swing an outcome that the same money could not move in a general election. This is why issue groups concentrate fire there.

blocks.text: In a House primary with **30,000 voters**, a $3M ad buy works out to roughly **$100 per voter reached** — an order of magnitude more saturation than a general election achieves.

timeline.heading: THE 314 ACTION ANGLE
timeline.body: 314 Action was founded in 2017 to recruit scientists and STEM professionals into Democratic politics — its name is a reference to pi. Its ostensibly issue-driven brand makes it a useful conduit: money arriving via 314 Action reads as pro-science endorsement rather than pro-Israel spending.

timeline.heading: THE DISCLOSURE LAG
timeline.body: FEC reports are filed quarterly, with pre-primary reports due 12 days before the election. Money that moves between committees in the final stretch often surfaces only after voters have cast ballots. Investigative tracing — following EDW Action Fund to 314 Action to a candidate — typically happens post-mortem.

timeline.heading: THE DURAND LINE
timeline.body: The 1893 border drawn by British colonial administrator Mortimer Durand cut the Pashtun homeland in half. Kabul has never formally recognized it. Tribes like the Wazir live on both sides, and the border is porous by geography and by tribal custom — which is why militant sanctuary in Afghanistan translates directly into attacks in Bannu.

blocks.label: the Pashtun belt straddles the Durand Line

timeline.heading: THE TRIBAL SYSTEM
timeline.body: Pashtun society organizes around the qaum (tribe) and the jirga — an assembly of elders that resolves disputes by consensus under Pashtunwali, the unwritten tribal code. For a century the Pakistani state governed these areas indirectly through tribal maliks, not police or courts.

blocks.text: The governing code is *Pashtunwali* — obligations of *melmastia* (hospitality), *nanawatai* (sanctuary for the supplicant), and *badal* (revenge). A killing without claim triggers badal obligations regardless of who the state blames.

timeline.heading: FATA'S MERGER
timeline.body: In 2018 Pakistan merged the Federally Administered Tribal Areas into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, ending the colonial-era Frontier Crimes Regulation. The legal integration was supposed to bring courts, police, and development. The security apparatus followed slower than the paperwork — the vacuum is where the TTP rebuilt.

timeline.heading: THE TTP RESURGENCE
timeline.body: Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan was battered by army operations in 2014-2016 and largely pushed into Afghanistan. After the Afghan Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021, TTP leadership returned to safe haven across the Durand Line. Attacks on Pakistani security forces and tribal elders in KP have roughly tripled since.

blocks.question: When did Pakistan merge the tribal areas (FATA) into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province?
options: 2022, after the Taliban takeover of Kabul
blocks.explanation: The 25th Amendment in 2018 dissolved FATA and its colonial-era Frontier Crimes Regulation, merging seven tribal agencies into KP province.

timeline.heading: WHY ELDERS ARE TARGETED
timeline.body: Pattern killings of tribal elders are not random terror — they are the deliberate decapitation of the jirga system. Every malik who cooperated with the state, or who raised a tribal lashkar (militia) against militants, becomes a target. Hollow out the elders and the tribe's collective bargaining power collapses.

timeline.heading: BANNU'S GEOGRAPHY
timeline.body: Bannu sits at the mouth of the Tochi Pass into North Waziristan — the main route militants use moving between the settled districts and the Afghan border. This is why the town has been a recurring flashpoint since the 2004 South Waziristan operations, not a new one.

2026-04-24-bannu-domel-abduction-killing.label: KP's Tribal Belt & the Security Vacuum

timeline.heading: THE DISTILLATION ACCUSATION
timeline.body: Training a frontier model from scratch costs hundreds of millions in compute. Distillation — querying a rival's model millions of times and training on its outputs — compresses that cost by orders of magnitude. The technique is well-documented; proving a specific competitor did it is nearly impossible without server-side query logs.

blocks.text: The legal term of art is **model distillation**. OpenAI's terms of service forbid using outputs to train a *competing* model — a contractual restriction, not a copyright one. No court has ruled on whether those terms survive cross-border enforcement.

timeline.heading: WHY OPEN WEIGHTS MATTER
timeline.body: DeepSeek releases model weights under permissive licenses. Anyone can run V4 on their own hardware, fine-tune it, or audit its behavior. OpenAI and Anthropic keep weights closed and serve only via API. The strategic implication: an open model becomes commodity infrastructure the moment it's released, compressing margins for closed competitors.

timeline.heading: THE EXPORT-CONTROL CONSTRAINT
timeline.body: US rules since 2022 bar Nvidia from selling its top-tier H100 and B200 chips to China. DeepSeek trained V3 on H800s — a deliberately hobbled export variant with throttled interconnect bandwidth. That constraint forced algorithmic efficiency gains Western labs never needed to pursue, because they could always throw more compute at the problem.

timeline.heading: THE TOKEN ECONOMICS
timeline.body: A 1-million-token context window means the model can read a full novel, a codebase, or a year of earnings calls in one shot. API pricing is per-token; DeepSeek's published rates are roughly one-tenth of GPT-4-class pricing. At scale, this is the difference between AI as a premium product and AI as utility infrastructure.

timeline.heading: THE SPUTNIK MOMENT
timeline.body: DeepSeek's R1 release in January 2025 wiped roughly $600 billion from Nvidia's market cap in a single day — the largest one-day loss in US stock market history. The thesis it broke: that compute scarcity alone would keep Chinese labs a generation behind. V4 is the follow-up data point.

blocks.question: What was novel about DeepSeek's R1 when it shocked markets in January 2025?
options: It was the first Chinese LLM
It matched frontier US models while trained on export-restricted chips
It was trained entirely without GPUs
It was the largest model ever released
blocks.explanation: R1 showed that algorithmic efficiency could compensate for hardware restrictions — breaking the assumption that US compute dominance guaranteed a capability lead.

timeline.heading: THE STATE-CAPITAL QUESTION
timeline.body: DeepSeek is nominally a private spinoff of the quant hedge fund High-Flyer, but no frontier Chinese AI lab operates without state alignment. Beijing's 2017 AI plan set a goal of global leadership by 2030; undercutting US pricing on open models serves that goal whether or not any direct subsidy exists.

2026-04-24-deepseek-v4-preview-china-us-.label: DeepSeek & the China AI Price War

timeline.heading: WHY LNG IS DIFFERENT
timeline.body: Unlike oil, natural gas cannot be rerouted by tanker from any port. Liquefying it requires chilling methane to -162°C in purpose-built export terminals that cost $10-20 billion and take 4-6 years to build. Destroy the terminal and the gas stays in the ground.

blocks.text: The industry term is *stranded gas* — reserves that physically exist but cannot reach market because the liquefaction infrastructure is gone or unbuilt.

timeline.heading: QATAR'S ONE EXIT
timeline.body: Qatar holds the world's third-largest gas reserves and exports nearly all of it as LNG through a single route: out of Ras Laffan, through the Strait of Hormuz, to Asia and Europe. There is no pipeline bypass. A Hormuz closure does not reduce Qatari exports gradually — it zeroes them.

timeline.heading: THE 120 BCM IN CONTEXT
timeline.body: Global LNG trade runs roughly 550 bcm per year. A 120 bcm loss by 2030 is more than a fifth of the market — larger than the entire output of the United States' LNG export industry before 2022.

timeline.heading: WHY REPAIRS TAKE YEARS
timeline.body: An LNG train — the cryogenic unit that liquefies gas — contains precision heat exchangers, compressors, and turbines made by a handful of firms worldwide (Air Products, Linde, Baker Hughes). Lead times for replacement equipment run 24-36 months even without a war. Add site clearance, engineering, and re-commissioning, and four years is optimistic.

timeline.heading: THE EUROPEAN EXPOSURE
timeline.body: After cutting Russian pipeline gas in 2022, Europe rebuilt its energy system around LNG imports — primarily from the US and Qatar. The TTF benchmark is now the price that sets German factory costs, Polish heating bills, and Italian power tariffs. A Qatari supply shock is a European industrial shock.

blocks.question: Before 2022, what share of EU natural gas came from Russia via pipeline?
blocks.explanation: Russia supplied roughly 40% of EU gas before the Ukraine invasion. Replacing it required record LNG imports and permanent demand destruction in heavy industry.

timeline.heading: THE IEA'S ROLE
timeline.body: The International Energy Agency was founded in 1974 by OECD countries after the Arab oil embargo, specifically to coordinate strategic reserves and forecast supply shocks. Its forecasts carry weight because member states are legally obligated to share inventory data — a transparency regime that does not exist for gas the way it does for oil.

timeline.heading: THE AADHAAR SUBSTRATE
timeline.body: India built the world's largest biometric database before it built the world's strongest privacy law. Aadhaar enrolled over 1.3 billion residents' fingerprints and iris scans starting in 2009; the Supreme Court only recognized privacy as a fundamental right in 2017, eight years after enrollment began.

blocks.text: The sequencing matters: in most democracies, *rights frameworks precede infrastructure*. India inverted that order — the rails were laid, then the rules were debated.

timeline.heading: THE PUTTASWAMY TEST
timeline.body: The 2017 Puttaswamy judgment set a four-part test for any state intrusion on privacy: legality, legitimate aim, proportionality, and procedural safeguards. Facial recognition deployments across Indian cities have never been tested against it — because no one has standing to sue until they can prove they were scanned.

timeline.heading: WHY SOFT LAW IS THE CHOICE
timeline.body: India's 2023 Digital Personal Data Protection Act exempts the state from most consent requirements when processing data for 'sovereign functions.' The AI framework follows the same architecture: obligations for private firms, broad discretion for the state. This is a design, not an oversight.

timeline.heading: THE PREDICTIVE-POLICING PROBLEM
timeline.body: Predictive policing systems trained on historical arrest data inherit the biases of who was policed before. In India, that means Dalits, Muslims, and tribal communities are overrepresented in training sets — and the models recommend more patrols in those neighborhoods, which produces more arrests, which retrains the model.

blocks.question: Why do predictive-policing models tend to amplify existing bias rather than correct it?
options: They train on past arrest data, creating a feedback loop
They are banned from using demographic variables
They rely on citizen reports rather than police data
blocks.explanation: Past arrests reflect where police patrolled, not where crime occurred. Training on that data teaches the model to recommend the same patrols — a closed loop.

timeline.heading: THE EU CONTRAST
timeline.body: The EU AI Act classifies remote biometric identification in public spaces as 'high-risk' or outright prohibited, with narrow law-enforcement carve-outs requiring judicial authorization. India's framework contains no equivalent category — the same technology is unrestricted by default.

timeline.heading: THE WELFARE LINK
timeline.body: India's welfare delivery runs on biometric authentication — ration shops, pensions, employment guarantees all verify identity via Aadhaar. When the AI layer fails to match a fingerprint or flags a household incorrectly, food stops arriving. Reported starvation deaths linked to authentication failures are the sharpest edge of the rights vacuum.

timeline.heading: THE BASIC MECHANISM
timeline.body: A stablecoin issuer holds reserve assets — typically US Treasury bills and bank deposits — and mints one token per dollar deposited. When you redeem, they burn the token and return the dollar. The token tracks $1 not by algorithm but by the promise and proof that the dollar is there.

blocks.text: The business is simple: issuers pocket the **yield on Treasuries** while paying token holders *nothing*. At 4%+ short rates, a $100bn float generates $4bn/yr in net interest income.

timeline.heading: WHY A BANK FUND MATTERS
timeline.body: Stablecoin issuers have historically self-custodied reserves or parked them at crypto-friendly banks. Silicon Valley Bank's 2023 collapse froze $3.3bn of Circle's USDC reserves over a weekend, briefly breaking the peg to 87 cents. A regulated money market vehicle at a systemically important bank removes that single-point-of-failure risk.

timeline.heading: THE GENIUS ACT
timeline.body: The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for US Stablecoins Act would require payment stablecoins to hold 1:1 reserves in cash, short Treasuries, or overnight repos — and bar algorithmic stablecoins from being marketed as payment tokens. It federalizes what New York's BitLicense did at state level.

timeline.heading: WHY REGULATORS CARE
timeline.body: When millions of people hold stablecoins that earn implicit yield via the issuer, that looks exactly like a money market fund — heavily regulated since the 1930s. A run on a major stablecoin would force fire-sales of Treasury bills, transmitting crypto stress directly into the short-end of the US government debt market.

blocks.question: What triggered USDC's brief depeg to $0.87 in March 2023?
options: $3.3bn of reserves stuck at failed Silicon Valley Bank
blocks.explanation: Circle disclosed SVB exposure on a Friday night; USDC traded off peg through the weekend until the FDIC backstopped uninsured deposits.

timeline.heading: THE DOLLAR DIMENSION
timeline.body: Stablecoin issuers now collectively hold over $120bn in US Treasuries — more than Germany or South Korea. Every dollar stablecoin minted abroad is a dollar of demand for US government debt, quietly extending dollar hegemony into jurisdictions where US banks cannot operate.

timeline.heading: THE SPRING MECHANISM
timeline.body: Tendons are not passive cables — they store and release elastic energy like a spring. In running, the Achilles tendon returns roughly 35% of the energy needed for each stride, reducing the metabolic cost of locomotion dramatically.

blocks.text: A stiffer tendon behaves like a *stiff spring*: it transmits force faster with less stretch, favoring **explosive** movement. A compliant tendon stretches more, storing energy over a longer stroke — better for **endurance**.

timeline.heading: WHY STIFFNESS MATTERS
timeline.body: Stiffness is force divided by elongation. A stiffer tendon transmits muscle force to bone with less delay, critical for jumping and sprinting. A more compliant tendon absorbs load over a longer window, protecting against repetitive strain in endurance work.

timeline.heading: THE ADAPTATION PRINCIPLE
timeline.body: Tendons remodel in response to mechanical loading, but far slower than muscle. Collagen turnover in the Achilles takes months to years, which is why tendon injuries — unlike muscle strains — heal on geological timescales by athletic standards.

timeline.heading: THE FEMALE ATHLETE GAP
timeline.body: Most sports science was built on male subjects. Women have different hormonal cycles, collagen synthesis rates, and injury patterns — ACL tears occur 4-6 times more often in women than men in equivalent sports. Sex-specific tendon research is finally catching up.

blocks.question: How much more frequently do ACL tears occur in female athletes versus males in comparable sports?
blocks.explanation: The disparity reflects differences in hip-knee alignment, hormonal effects on ligament laxity, and neuromuscular activation patterns.

timeline.heading: NETBALL VS DISTANCE RUNNING
timeline.body: Netball demands repeated jumps, sudden stops, and lateral cuts on a hard court — brief, high-force loading. Distance running is sustained, rhythmic, lower-force loading over thousands of strides. The tendons adapt to what they are asked to do.

timeline.heading: BODY MASS NORMALIZATION
timeline.body: Raw tendon thickness scales with body size — bigger athletes have bigger tendons. Dividing by body mass reveals whether a tissue is disproportionately adapted or just proportionally larger. Most apparent sport differences in anatomy vanish under this correction.

timeline.heading: THE COUP BELT
timeline.body: Since 2020, West Africa has seen successful coups in Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea, Niger, and Gabon — a contiguous arc from the Atlantic to Lake Chad. Nigeria, the region's anchor, is the last large democracy in a neighborhood that has tipped.

timeline.heading: NIGERIA'S OWN HISTORY
timeline.body: Between independence in 1960 and the return of civilian rule in 1999, Nigeria experienced six successful coups and several failed attempts. Every head of state for 29 of those 39 years came to power through the barracks, not the ballot box.

blocks.text: The 1966 coup that killed Prime Minister Tafawa Balewa triggered pogroms against Igbos in the north — and ultimately the **Biafran War**, which killed over a million people before federal forces crushed the secession in 1970.

timeline.heading: WHY THE COURT MARTIAL
timeline.body: Nigerian military law tries serving officers via General Court Martial under the Armed Forces Act. Civilians and retired officers go to Federal High Court. The split jurisdiction is deliberate — it preserves civilian oversight of military justice while keeping operational discipline within the chain of command.

timeline.heading: THE AIR FORCE TELL
timeline.body: Successful African coups almost always involve the army's ground forces — tanks and infantry seizing the capital. When air force officers are implicated, it usually signals a plot to neutralize the president's movement: grounding the presidential fleet, closing airspace, or strafing loyalist columns. An air vice-marshal in the dock is a structural signal.

blocks.question: Which branch's involvement in a coup plot typically signals intent to neutralize presidential mobility?
blocks.explanation: Air force involvement targets the president's ability to move — grounding aircraft, closing airspace — while ground forces seize the capital.

timeline.heading: THE TINUBU CONTEXT
timeline.body: President Bola Tinubu took office in May 2023 and immediately removed the fuel subsidy and floated the naira. The naira has lost roughly two-thirds of its value against the dollar since; inflation peaked above 30%. Economic pain and coup plotting historically correlate in Nigeria — the 1983 Buhari coup cited exactly this pattern.

timeline.heading: THE DEMOCRATIC STAKES
timeline.body: Nigeria is 220 million people, Africa's largest economy by most measures, and the continent's largest oil producer. A successful coup in Abuja would not just add one more flag to the Sahel belt — it would end the assumption that democratic consolidation, once achieved, is irreversible.

timeline.heading: THE CITY'S STRATEGIC WEIGHT
timeline.body: Odesa is Ukraine's last major Black Sea port. Before the 2022 invasion it handled roughly two-thirds of Ukrainian grain exports — wheat, corn, sunflower oil that fed North Africa and the Middle East. Strikes on Odesa are strikes on the global food supply chain.

timeline.heading: THE SHAHED ECONOMY
timeline.body: Russia's workhorse strike drone is the Iranian-designed Shahed-136, now mass-produced in Tatarstan as the Geran-2. Unit cost is estimated at $20,000–50,000. A Patriot interceptor fired to shoot one down costs roughly $4 million. The asymmetry is the weapon.

blocks.text: The drones fly low, slow, and loud — nicknamed *mopeds* by Ukrainians for the lawnmower buzz of their engines. Cheap to build, cheap to launch, expensive to stop.

timeline.heading: THE TERROR DOCTRINE
timeline.body: Strikes on residential buildings are not misfires. Russian doctrine since the Chechen wars — Grozny 1999, Aleppo 2016 — treats civilian infrastructure as a legitimate pressure point on enemy morale. The targeting is the message.

blocks.question: Which Russian campaign established the modern playbook of strikes on urban civilian targets?
blocks.explanation: Grozny's near-total destruction in 1999–2000 became the template later applied in Aleppo and across Ukraine.

timeline.heading: THE BLACK SEA LAUNCH
timeline.body: Drones launched from Russian-held Crimea or Black Sea vessels reach Odesa in minutes. The short flight path defeats layered air defense — by the time radar picks up a low-flying Shahed over the water, interception windows are measured in seconds.

timeline.heading: THE HUMAN LEDGER
timeline.body: The UN has verified over 13,000 Ukrainian civilian deaths since February 2022, with actual figures likely far higher. The elderly are overrepresented — they cannot shelter quickly, and many refuse to leave homes they have lived in for decades.

timeline.heading: THE C–H PROBLEM
timeline.body: Most carbon-hydrogen bonds in organic molecules are nearly identical in strength and shape. Selectively breaking one specific C–H bond — while leaving dozens of others untouched — is one of the hardest problems in synthesis. Traditional routes install a reactive group first, then swap it; every step loses yield.

blocks.text: Chemists call this the **selectivity problem**: reactions that touch the wrong C–H bond produce isomers that are chemically similar but biologically useless — or toxic.

timeline.heading: ATOM ECONOMY
timeline.body: Coined by Barry Trost in 1991, atom economy measures how many atoms from the starting materials end up in the final product. Classical amino acid synthesis discards most of the inputs as salt waste. Grabbing a CO2 molecule from the air and welding it directly onto a C–H bond is the theoretical ceiling — nothing wasted.

timeline.heading: WHY CO2 IS HARD TO USE
timeline.body: CO2 is the thermodynamic end-state of combustion — it is what everything burns into. Pushing it backward into a carbon-carbon bond requires injecting energy equivalent to undoing the burn. Photons from a UV lamp provide exactly this energy, which is why photoredox chemistry unlocked reactions that heat alone cannot drive.

timeline.heading: THE DIRECTING GROUP TRICK
timeline.body: A thioamide is a sulfur-containing tag attached near the target C–H bond. Sulfur loosely binds the photocatalyst, holding it in place so it activates only the nearby bond. After the reaction, the tag is removed. This is the same logic Nobel-winning palladium catalysis used — proximity beats intrinsic reactivity.

blocks.question: Why do chemists attach a 'directing group' before a selective C–H reaction?
options: To make the molecule more soluble in water
To hold the catalyst near one specific bond among many similar ones
To protect the molecule from oxygen during the reaction
To increase the overall yield by adding mass
blocks.explanation: Directing groups solve the selectivity problem by physically tethering the catalyst next to the target bond — proximity, not intrinsic reactivity, decides which C–H bond reacts.

timeline.heading: WHY AMINO ACIDS
timeline.body: Roughly a third of all FDA-approved small-molecule drugs contain a non-natural amino acid or a peptide fragment. The 20 amino acids biology provides are not enough — medicinal chemists need custom side chains to tune potency and half-life. A general route from cheap feedstock plus CO2 is a direct cost lever on drug manufacturing.

timeline.heading: STERIC EFFECTS
timeline.body: Bulky groups near a reactive site physically block the catalyst from approaching. Many elegant reactions fail on drug molecules specifically because drug candidates are crowded — the interesting C–H bonds are the ones surrounded by other atoms. A method that works on crowded substrates is worth more than one that works only on simple test cases.

timeline.heading: THE DOMESTIC DEBT TRAP
timeline.body: Pakistan's public debt is roughly 70% of GDP, and more than half is domestic. Because foreign lenders won't lend in rupees at tolerable rates, the state borrows from its own banks — which then hold so much government paper that they have little balance-sheet room for private credit.

blocks.text: Economists call this *financial repression* — when banks are effectively required to fund the state, **crowding out** private borrowers and suppressing investment.

timeline.heading: WHAT A BUYBACK ACTUALLY DOES
timeline.body: The State Bank uses cash to retire bonds before they mature. This lowers the government's future interest bill, shortens the debt stock's duration, and frees capacity on bank balance sheets to absorb fresh issuance — a rollover lubricated in advance rather than scrambled at maturity.

timeline.heading: FLOATING-RATE EXPOSURE
timeline.body: The bonds being retired are Pakistan Investment Bonds with coupons pegged to the 6-month T-bill rate. When the policy rate was 22% in 2024, these instruments bled the budget. As the SBP cuts rates, retiring floaters locks in the savings rather than waiting for them to accrue.

timeline.heading: THE IMF SHADOW
timeline.body: Pakistan is inside a $7bn Extended Fund Facility signed in 2024 — its 24th IMF programme since 1958. Debt-management operations like buybacks are part of the fiscal discipline the Fund tracks quarterly; interest costs consume nearly half of federal revenue.

timeline.heading: WHY THE RUPEE MATTERS
timeline.body: Domestic debt is rupee-denominated, but Pakistan's external debt — roughly $130bn — is not. Every rupee of depreciation against the dollar inflates the external debt stock measured in local currency. Managing the domestic stack is only half the problem.

blocks.question: Roughly what share of Pakistan's federal revenue goes to interest payments on public debt?
blocks.explanation: Debt servicing consumes close to half of federal revenue, leaving little for development spending — the core reason IMF programmes keep recurring.

timeline.heading: THE STRUCTURAL BIND
timeline.body: Pakistan's tax-to-GDP ratio hovers near 10% — among the lowest in Asia. Without a broader tax base, every rate cut and every buyback is tactical relief on a strategic problem: the state collects too little to fund itself without borrowing.

timeline.heading: THE ENGINE
timeline.body: Warm, salty surface water flows north from the tropics, cools near Greenland and Iceland, grows dense, and sinks. That sinking pulls more warm water behind it. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation is this conveyor — heat moving north on the surface, cold water returning south at depth.

blocks.text: The system runs on **density**, not wind. Cold plus salty equals heavy; heavy water sinks; sinking drives the loop. Break the density contrast and the engine stalls.

timeline.heading: THE SALT PROBLEM
timeline.body: Greenland's ice sheet is losing roughly 270 billion tonnes of freshwater per year. That meltwater dilutes the North Atlantic's surface salinity, making it less dense. Less dense water does not sink. Less sinking means a slower conveyor — and a slower conveyor transports less salt north, further reducing density. The feedback is what makes a tipping point possible.

timeline.heading: THE YOUNGER DRYAS PRECEDENT
timeline.body: Roughly 12,900 years ago, a massive pulse of meltwater from a North American glacial lake flooded the Atlantic. Within decades, temperatures in Greenland dropped by 10°C and Europe plunged back into near-glacial cold for about 1,200 years. The paleoclimate record is why scientists take AMOC collapse seriously — it has happened before, and it happened fast.

timeline.heading: WHAT EUROPE LOSES
timeline.body: AMOC delivers roughly the thermal equivalent of a million nuclear power plants to the North Atlantic. It is why Edinburgh (56°N) has mild winters while Moscow (55°N) is frozen solid, and why palm trees grow in Cornwall at the latitude of Labrador. A collapse would not mean gradual cooling — it would mean European winters resembling Canadian ones within a generation.

blocks.question: London and which city sit at roughly the same latitude?
blocks.explanation: London is at 51°N — the same as Calgary. AMOC warmth is why one has mild drizzle and the other has −30°C winters.

timeline.heading: THE SAHEL CONNECTION
timeline.body: A weaker AMOC shifts the Intertropical Convergence Zone — the tropical rain belt — southward. Paleoclimate records show that past AMOC slowdowns coincided with catastrophic droughts across the Sahel and West African monsoon failure. The circulation that warms Europe also waters Nigeria and Senegal.

timeline.heading: THE DISPUTE
timeline.body: The IPCC considers a full 21st-century collapse unlikely but cannot rule it out. Some 2023–2024 papers using salinity records argue the tipping point could arrive as early as mid-century; others using ocean models see continued weakening without collapse. The disagreement is about model confidence, not about whether the system is slowing — that part is settled.

timeline.heading: THE OPEN-WEIGHTS STRATEGY
timeline.body: DeepSeek releases model weights under permissive licenses — anyone can download, fine-tune, and self-host. This is the opposite of OpenAI and Anthropic, whose frontier models are accessible only via API. Open weights turn a model into infrastructure; closed weights keep it a service.

blocks.text: The strategic logic: if a Chinese lab cannot out-spend US hyperscalers, it can **commoditize** the layer they monetize. Every open-source release erodes the pricing power of *closed* frontier labs.

timeline.heading: THE MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS TRICK
timeline.body: A 1.6-trillion-parameter model does not activate all parameters per token. Mixture-of-Experts architectures route each token to a small subset — often 30-40 billion active parameters — giving the capacity of a huge model at the inference cost of a small one. This is how DeepSeek undercuts US pricing without matching US compute budgets.

timeline.heading: THE EXPORT CONTROL GAP
timeline.body: October 2022 US controls banned exports of Nvidia's top AI chips (H100, later H200, B200) to China. Nvidia designed cut-down variants (H800, H20) to stay under the threshold; those were banned in 2023 and 2025. Huawei's Ascend 910C is China's domestic answer — slower per chip, but available in volume.

blocks.label: AI training chips, rough peak FP16

timeline.heading: THE COST COLLAPSE
timeline.body: DeepSeek's V3, released late 2024, claimed a $6M training run — roughly a fiftieth of what GPT-4-class models were rumored to cost. The number is contested (it excludes prior research compute), but the direction is real: algorithmic efficiency is compounding faster than hardware is scaling.

blocks.question: Why does open-sourcing a frontier model hurt closed-model labs more than it hurts DeepSeek?
options: DeepSeek earns most revenue from cloud services, not API calls
Open-weight models are banned from commercial use
DeepSeek is subsidized by the Chinese state
Open models always outperform closed ones
blocks.explanation: Closed labs like OpenAI monetize per-token API access; open weights let anyone self-host, collapsing that pricing power. DeepSeek's parent is a quant hedge fund — the lab is not its revenue engine.

timeline.heading: THE HEDGE FUND ORIGIN
timeline.body: DeepSeek was spun out of High-Flyer, a Chinese quantitative hedge fund that built a 10,000-GPU cluster for trading before pivoting to AI research in 2023. It is not a typical venture-funded startup — there is no pressure to monetize the model itself, which is why giving it away is viable.

timeline.heading: WHY BENCHMARKS MISLEAD
timeline.body: Coding benchmarks like HumanEval and SWE-bench are public, which means frontier labs optimize against them directly. A model that 'matches GPT-class' on benchmarks may still lag on the long-tail reasoning, tool-use, and reliability that define real deployments. Benchmark parity is a floor, not a ceiling.

timeline.heading: THE JURISDICTION TRICK
timeline.body: The Rome Statute lets the ICC prosecute crimes committed while a state was a member — even if the state later withdraws. Duterte took the Philippines out in 2019, but the court retained authority over killings between 2011 (when Manila joined) and March 2019 (when withdrawal took effect).

blocks.text: This is why Duterte's defense strategy of *ratione temporis* — arguing the court lost jurisdiction at withdrawal — failed. The **Rome Statute Article 127** explicitly preserves pending matters.

timeline.heading: THE BODY COUNT
timeline.body: Philippine police reported about 6,200 deaths in official anti-drug operations from 2016 to 2022. Human rights groups, counting vigilante killings the government disclaimed, put the real figure at 12,000 to 30,000. The gap between the two numbers is itself the case against him — the ICC charges rest on a policy of tolerated extrajudicial killing, not just documented raids.

blocks.question: What is the lowest officially-acknowledged death toll from Duterte's drug war?
blocks.explanation: Philippine National Police records ~6,200 killed in sanctioned operations; rights groups estimate the true toll including vigilante killings is several times higher.

timeline.heading: THE DAVAO BLUEPRINT
timeline.body: Before the presidency, Duterte spent two decades as mayor of Davao City, where the 'Davao Death Squad' was linked to over 1,400 killings of suspected criminals and street children. The 2016 national campaign was an explicit scaling of that model — he ran on it, openly.

timeline.heading: WHY THE ICC RARELY REACHES HEADS OF STATE
timeline.body: The court has indicted sitting or former leaders before — Bashir of Sudan, Gaddafi, Putin — but almost none have seen trial. Duterte is unusual: his own successor's government allowed his arrest and transfer. Most heads of state are shielded by the state itself.

blocks.label: former heads of state indicted by the ICC

timeline.heading: THE MARCOS FACTOR
timeline.body: Duterte's surrender was possible because the Marcos-Duterte political alliance collapsed after 2024. The same Marcos family once shielded by martial-law immunity now permits a former ally to face The Hague — a reminder that international justice usually arrives through domestic political fracture, not international pressure.

timeline.heading: CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY, DEFINED
timeline.body: The legal threshold is a 'widespread or systematic attack directed against a civilian population' pursuant to a state or organizational policy. Individual murders are domestic crimes; a policy of murders is a crime against humanity. The ICC's task is proving the pattern, not any single killing.

timeline.heading: WHAT THE PREMIUM IS
timeline.body: Oil futures price in the probability of supply disruption, not just current supply and demand. When traders assign a nonzero chance that a chokepoint closes, every barrel globally gets more expensive — even barrels that never pass near the threatened strait.

blocks.text: Analysts decompose crude into a **fundamentals price** (supply, demand, inventories) and a **risk premium** (geopolitical probability weighting). The premium can swing $10–20/bbl in days while fundamentals barely move.

timeline.heading: THE HORMUZ WEIGHT
timeline.body: Roughly 21 million barrels per day transit the Strait of Hormuz — about a fifth of global oil consumption. The shipping lanes are just 3 km wide each, hugging the Iranian coast. No alternate route exists for most Gulf producers at anywhere near the same volume.

timeline.heading: THE TANKER WAR PRECEDENT
timeline.body: From 1984 to 1988, Iran and Iraq attacked more than 400 commercial ships in the Gulf. Prices spiked but markets adapted — tankers were reflagged under US and Kuwaiti flags and escorted by warships. The lesson planners took: disruption is easier to threaten than to sustain.

timeline.heading: WHY IRANIAN CRUDE IS DISCOUNTED
timeline.body: Sanctioned Iranian barrels usually trade $10–15 below Brent because buyers — primarily Chinese independent refiners — demand compensation for sanctions risk, shadow-fleet logistics, and payment workarounds. When Iranian crude approaches Brent, the discount is collapsing because the marginal buyer thinks sanctions enforcement is weakening.

timeline.heading: WHO ACTUALLY PAYS
timeline.body: The US imports almost no Persian Gulf oil — shale made it a net exporter. But oil is priced on a single global market, so a Hormuz scare raises pump prices everywhere. Treaty allies face the sharpest squeeze.

timeline.heading: THE INSURANCE CHOKEPOINT
timeline.body: Lloyd's of London war-risk premiums — not missiles — are what actually close a shipping lane. Once underwriters reclassify a waterway, commercial vessels reroute regardless of whether any ship has been hit. The financial chokepoint tightens before the physical one does.

blocks.question: What most directly determines whether tankers keep transiting a contested strait?
blocks.explanation: Marine insurers set war-risk rates daily. When premiums spike past a threshold, charters become uneconomic and ships reroute — even if the strait is physically open.

timeline.heading: WHAT EPR ACTUALLY DOES
timeline.body: Extended Producer Responsibility shifts the cost of end-of-life waste from municipalities to the companies that put packaging on the market. Producers either pay a per-tonne fee into a collection fund or must demonstrate they recovered an equivalent weight. The mechanism is borrowed from Germany's 1991 Packaging Ordinance, which cut packaging waste by a third within a decade.

blocks.text: The core idea: **internalize the externality**. If making a plastic bottle is cheap only because disposal is someone else's problem, force the producer to pay the disposal cost — and watch them redesign the bottle.

timeline.heading: THE INVISIBLE WORKFORCE
timeline.body: Roughly 40,000 pickers — many of them Afghan refugees, Pashtun migrants, and children — do the actual work of recovering plastic in Karachi. They sort at dumpsites, sell to middlemen called kabaris, and collectively process more material than any formal facility in the country. No contracts, no protective gear, no legal recognition.

timeline.heading: THE INDIA PRECEDENT
timeline.body: India's 2022 Plastic Waste Management Rules introduced EPR targets for producers and brand owners. A 2024 audit by the Centre for Science and Environment found 59% of registered producers missed their recovery targets in the first two cycles. Enforcement fell to state pollution control boards that were already understaffed — the targets existed on paper but penalties rarely landed.

timeline.heading: WHY FORMALIZATION IS HARD
timeline.body: Pickers earn more in the informal economy than most formal recycling jobs would pay, because middlemen compete for their output and pay cash daily. Formal systems require IDs, bank accounts, and fixed hours — all barriers for migrants without documents. Bogotá and Belo Horizonte are the rare cities that integrated pickers into municipal contracts; both took over a decade of organized cooperative bargaining.

blocks.question: Which country's EPR system most successfully integrated informal waste pickers into the formal recycling economy?
options: Germany, via the Green Dot system
Brazil, via picker cooperatives recognized by federal decree
blocks.explanation: Brazil's 2010 National Solid Waste Policy legally recognized catador cooperatives as priority contractors for municipal recycling — the template cited in picker organizing worldwide.

timeline.heading: THE FREE-RIDER PROBLEM
timeline.body: EPR only works if every producer pays. When enforcement is weak, compliant companies subsidize the rest — raising their costs while cheaters keep market share. This is why EPR laws succeed in jurisdictions with strong regulatory capacity and fail in those without. The law's text is the easy part; the audit trail is where it lives or dies.

timeline.heading: WHAT ROSKOMNADZOR IS
timeline.body: Roskomnadzor — the Federal Service for Supervision of Communications — is Russia's internet censor. It maintains the blacklist of blocked sites, enforces the 2019 'sovereign internet' law requiring ISPs to install deep-packet inspection boxes, and throttles or blocks foreign platforms. After February 2022 it blocked Facebook, Instagram, and most Western news sites within weeks.

blocks.text: The agency is the civilian face of Russia's information control; the **FSB** is the coercive one. A plot against Roskomnadzor leadership attacks the bureaucratic machine, not the intelligence apparatus.

timeline.heading: WHY TELEGRAM
timeline.body: Telegram is the dominant messaging app in both Russia and Ukraine — roughly 80% penetration in each. Its channels carry everything from military recruitment to front-line reporting. Russian authorities repeatedly claim Ukrainian intelligence uses it to recruit disaffected Russians for sabotage; Ukrainian services acknowledge running influence operations there. The same app both sides use to talk is the app both sides use to recruit.

blocks.question: Why hasn't Russia blocked Telegram, unlike other foreign platforms?
options: Telegram's founder cooperates with the FSB
Russian officials, military, and pro-war bloggers depend on it themselves
It is hosted on Russian servers
A 2018-2020 blocking attempt failed and was reversed
blocks.explanation: Roskomnadzor tried to block Telegram from 2018 to 2020 and failed — the app rerouted around blocks while collateral damage hit other services. The climbdown is why Telegram still runs freely in Russia.

timeline.heading: THE FSB'S DUAL ROLE
timeline.body: The Federal Security Service is both Russia's domestic intelligence agency and the primary successor to the KGB's Second Chief Directorate. It investigates terrorism, runs counterintelligence, and — since 2003 — controls the border guards. Announcing a foiled plot serves two purposes at once: demonstrating competence and justifying expanded surveillance powers.

timeline.heading: THE RECRUITMENT PATTERN
timeline.body: Since 2022, Russia has announced dozens of foiled sabotage and assassination plots attributed to Ukrainian handlers recruiting Russian citizens online. The targets have included military commissariats, railway signal boxes, defense industry executives, and pro-war bloggers. Recruits are typically young, financially stressed, and contacted through Telegram offers of payment for 'small tasks' that escalate.

timeline.heading: THE CHARGE
timeline.body: Russia's terrorism statute (Article 205 of the Criminal Code) carries up to life imprisonment, with a 15-year minimum for organized acts. Since 2022, prosecutors have used it aggressively for sabotage cases that would historically have been charged as vandalism or weapons offenses. Convictions in these cases run above 99%.

blocks.text: Under 2022 amendments, 'discrediting the armed forces' and 'state treason' were also broadened — treason now covers 'providing assistance' to a foreign state deemed hostile, a standard vague enough to catch a Telegram message.

timeline.heading: WHY PUBLICIZE
timeline.body: Foiled-plot announcements are a recurring feature of wartime Russian media. They reinforce the narrative that Ukraine — not Russia — is the aggressor, justify continued mobilization, and give the FSB budgetary leverage. Soviet-era precedent runs deep: the KGB regularly surfaced 'foiled Western plots' at moments of political need, a pattern Russian security services have preserved.
